source.title: Optimal Implicit Bias in Linear Regression

record.tranche_reason: The paper mentions and cites double descent as background, but its analysis and results concern asymptotic generalization risk and implicit bias for over-parameterized linear regression. It does not test any of the listed double-descent versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports excess-risk comparisons among interpolators across over-parameterization ratios and noise settings (Section 4, Figures 2 and 5). The text does not report a fall-rise-fall curve or test behavior across the interpolation threshold; its setup assumes the over-parameterized regime. The comparisons below are relevant to generalization risk but do not measure any listed claim version.
record.test_reason: Double descent is named only as background in the introduction. All results concern the excess risk of convex-potential interpolators in the over-parameterized linear regime (0<δ=m/n<1). Nothing sweeps across the interpolation threshold, over epochs, or across complexity counts. No result bears on whether V1–V7 hold.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. The authors give precise asymptotics for the risk of convex-potential interpolators in over-parameterized linear regression. They give a tight Fisher-information-based lower bound and construct an optimal convex implicit bias under log-concavity conditions. They leave non-asymptotic and nonlinear extensions to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies optimal implicit bias for linear-regression interpolators; it does not reproduce the original double-descent studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported interpolator comparisons vary with signal prior, noise level, covariance structure, and over-parameterization ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: The isotropic lower bound is σ²/(1−δ)+(1−δ)/I(B). The authors say increasing δ toward 1 recovers more signal but amplifies the noise from overfitting. This is an analytic tension within the over-parameterized side only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In proportional-asymptotic linear interpolation, the best achievable risk of any convex-potential interpolator trades noise amplification (diverging as δ→1) against signal recovery.

fits_no_version.finding: The relative excess risk of min-ℓ1, ℓ2, ℓ3 and ℓ∞ interpolators depends on the signal prior and the SNR. The min-ℓ2 interpolator is near the lower bound for sparse-Gaussian signals, and near it for Gaussian signals at high SNR only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The generalization of interpolating solutions depends on the implicit bias matched to signal prior and noise level.

record.problems: The reported interpolator comparisons do not test the double-descent versions. The text gives qualitative descriptions of the risk plots rather than numerical values or uncertainty estimates, and the analysis is restricted to the over-parameterized linear-regression setting.

untested.parts: No sample sweep across or near m=n. δ is restricted to (0,1), and Figure 2 shows only qualitative interpolator comparisons.
No capacity sweep from under- to over-parameterized for any model class.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
Noise level changes the relative ranking of interpolators. No peak, peak splitting, or tuned-regularization removal is measured.

record.verdict_notes: Corollary 3.5's σ²/(1−δ) term diverges as δ→1, which is related to the interpolation-threshold peak. It is a bound restricted to δ<1 and drawn from Muthukumar et al., so it is not treated as a test of V3 or V6. The Figure 5 empirical-vs-theory risk curves (d=3000) were also not rowed; they validate the theory and do not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep testing the stated curve or its peak near the training-fit threshold.
No increase in sample count near the interpolation threshold is tested for its effect on test error.
No capacity sweep across the interpolation point is reported, even for the linear-regression setting.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak location across axes.
Noise levels are compared for interpolator risks, but the paper does not test whether noise drives a double-descent peak, whether peaks split, or whether tuned regularization removes a peak.
No re-counting of complexity or test of whether that turns a second descent into a U-shaped curve.

relation.reason: Although double descent is named as background, Equations (7) and (12), with Corollary 3.8, provide an analytical result bearing on V3: at fixed positive noise, increasing delta toward one eventually increases risk. This is an inference from the paper's risk formula.

tranche.reason: The paper's own asymptotic results bear on V3 in its linear-regression setting. Corollary 3.5 gives an exact Gaussian-prior risk expression, attained by the isotropic minimum-l2 interpolator through Corollary 3.8. Its risk increases with the sample-to-parameter ratio sufficiently near the interpolation threshold. This implication does not require crossing the threshold.

source_check.notes: Missing V3 result: for isotropic data and B~N(0,1), optimal minimum-l2 population risk is sigma^2/(1-delta)+(1-delta), implying more-data harm sufficiently near delta=1 at positive noise. Figure 2 reports numerical evaluations of asymptotic formulas; its eight comparator rows do not capture this result.
